label: ICT: set 3 (networks, the Internet and email, mobile technology, computer ethics, viruses and cybersecurity)

papers.title: Networks and Networking: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on networks and networking, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The computers in one school's laboratory, linked to share a printer and files, form
questions.explanation:
A LAN covers a small area such as a room, a building or a school compound, and is usually owned by one organisation.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a wide area network (WAN): A WAN covers countries or continents, not one building.
- a metropolitan area network (MAN): A MAN covers a whole town or city.
- a personal area network (PAN): A PAN links one person's devices within a few metres.

questions.stem: In which topology does a break in the single main cable stop the whole network?
questions.explanation:
In a bus topology every node shares one backbone cable with a terminator at each end, so a break in the backbone stops all communication.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- star: In a star, a broken cable cuts off only the computer on that cable.
- mesh: A mesh has many routes, so it keeps working if one link fails.
- tree: A tree joins several stars; a break affects only part of it.

questions.stem: Which device sends data only to the computer it is addressed to, rather than to every computer on the network?
questions.explanation:
A switch reads the address on each piece of data and forwards it only to the right device, making the network faster and more private than one built on a hub.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a hub: A hub sends every message out to all connected devices.
- a repeater: A repeater only boosts a weak signal.
- a modem: A modem converts signals for a telephone, cable or mobile line.

questions.stem: Which transmission medium carries data as pulses of light?
questions.explanation:
Fibre-optic cable sends pulses of light along thin glass fibres. It is very fast, works over long distances and is not affected by electrical interference.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- twisted-pair cable: Twisted pair carries electrical signals on copper wires.
- coaxial cable: Coaxial cable carries electrical signals on a copper core.
- microwave link: Microwaves are radio waves beamed through the air.

questions.stem: Communication between two walkie-talkies, where only one person can speak at a time, is an example of
questions.explanation:
In half-duplex transmission data travels in both directions, but only one way at a time.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simplex transmission: Simplex sends in one direction only, as in radio broadcasting.
- full-duplex transmission: Full duplex lets both sides send at the same time, as in a phone call.
- parallel transmission: Parallel transmission sends several bits at once along separate wires.

questions.stem: A device that connects a school's local network to the Internet and chooses the path for data between networks is
questions.explanation:
A router joins different networks, such as a LAN and the Internet, and directs data along the best path between them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a network interface card: A NIC connects a single device to a network.
- a hub: A hub only joins devices within one network.
- a repeater: A repeater boosts signals but makes no routing decisions.

questions.stem: In which type of network is every computer equal, sharing its own files directly with the others?
questions.explanation:
In a peer-to-peer network there is no central server; each computer shares its own resources. It suits small networks of a few computers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a client-server network: A client-server network depends on a central server.
- a wide area network: WAN describes the area covered, not how computers share.
- a star network: Star describes the layout of the cables, not how computers share.

papers.title: The Internet and Email: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the internet and email, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.explanation:
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, linking pages across the Internet with hyperlinks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Bill Gates: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft.
- Charles Babbage: Babbage designed mechanical computers in the 1800s.
- Steve Jobs: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple.

questions.stem: Which system translates a domain name such as example.com into an IP address?
questions.explanation:
DNS works like a directory: it looks up the domain name a person types and returns the IP address computers use to find the server.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- HTTPS: HTTPS is the secure protocol for sending web pages.
- an Internet service provider: An ISP connects customers to the Internet.
- a search engine: A search engine finds web pages that match key words.

questions.stem: In the web address https://www.example.org/news.html, which part is the top-level domain?
questions.explanation:
The top-level domain is the last part of the domain name, here .org, used mainly by organisations.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- https: https is the protocol.
- www: www is the host.
- news.html: news.html is the page at the end of the path.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a web browser?
questions.explanation:
Web browsers include Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Safari and Opera Mini.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Google Search: Google Search is a search engine, used inside a browser.
- Microsoft Outlook: Outlook is an email program.
- WhatsApp: WhatsApp is a messaging app.

questions.stem: A student wants a teacher to receive a copy of an email without the other recipients seeing the teacher's address. The teacher's address should go in the
questions.explanation:
BCC (blind carbon copy) sends a copy while hiding that address from the other recipients.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- CC field: Addresses in CC are visible to every recipient.
- To field: Addresses in To are visible to every recipient.
- Subject field: The subject holds the title of the message, not addresses.

questions.stem: Copying a file from a website onto your own phone is called
questions.explanation:
Downloading copies data from the Internet to your device; uploading sends data from your device to the Internet.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- uploading: Uploading sends a file from your device to the Internet.
- browsing: Browsing is viewing web pages.
- forwarding: Forwarding sends a received email on to someone else.

questions.stem: A private network that works like the Internet but is open only to the staff of one organisation is called
questions.explanation:
An intranet uses Internet technology, such as web pages and email, inside one organisation, and outsiders cannot reach it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an extranet: An extranet also lets chosen outsiders, such as suppliers, log in.
- the World Wide Web: The Web is public, open to anyone with a browser.
- a search engine: A search engine is a website for finding pages.

papers.title: Mobile Technology and ICT Gadgets: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on mobile technology and ict gadgets, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: SMS text messaging was introduced with which generation of mobile networks?
questions.explanation:
2G (GSM) networks of the 1990s made calls digital and introduced SMS text messages.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1G: 1G carried analogue voice calls only.
- 3G: 3G added mobile Internet and video calls; SMS already existed.
- 4G: 4G added fast mobile broadband.

questions.stem: The 15-digit number that identifies a mobile phone handset, shown by dialling *#06#, is the
questions.explanation:
The IMEI (International Mobile Equipment Identity) stays with the phone; operators can use it to block a stolen handset.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- SIM number: The SIM identifies the subscriber, not the handset.
- PIN: A PIN is a secret code chosen by the user.
- IP address: An IP address identifies a device on a network connection, not the handset itself.

questions.stem: Which technology lets a phone connect to wireless earphones over a short distance?
questions.explanation:
Bluetooth is a short-range radio technology, about 10 metres, for linking nearby devices without cables.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- GPS: GPS uses satellites to find position.
- USSD: USSD is a menu service reached by dialling short codes.
- 4G: 4G connects a phone to the mobile network's masts.

questions.stem: Which feature lets a smartphone share its mobile data connection with a laptop by Wi-Fi?
questions.explanation:
Turning on the hotspot makes the phone act as a small Wi-Fi access point for other devices, using its mobile data.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- near-field communication (NFC): NFC works over a few centimetres, for contactless payment.
- the accelerometer: The accelerometer detects movement and tilt.
- GPS: GPS finds the phone's position.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT usually done with mobile money?
questions.explanation:
Mobile money is used to send and receive money, pay bills, buy airtime, pay in shops and withdraw cash from agents. Printing is done with a computer and printer.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- paying an electricity bill: Bill payment is a common mobile money service.
- sending money to a relative: Sending money is the main use of mobile money.
- buying airtime: Airtime can be bought from a mobile money account.

questions.stem: Everyday objects such as meters, cameras and lights fitted with sensors and connected to the Internet make up
questions.explanation:
In the Internet of Things, objects send data and can be controlled remotely, such as smart meters and security cameras viewed on a phone.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the World Wide Web: The Web is linked pages of information, not connected objects.
- a personal area network: A PAN is a few devices around one person.
- an intranet: An intranet is a private network of one organisation.

questions.stem: A wearable gadget that counts steps and shows messages from a phone is
questions.explanation:
Smartwatches and fitness bands are wearables: they track steps and heartbeat and show notifications from a paired phone, usually by Bluetooth.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an e-reader: An e-reader is for reading electronic books.
- a power bank: A power bank stores charge for recharging devices.
- a drone: A drone is a remote-controlled flying device.

papers.title: Computer Ethics: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on computer ethics, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Installing one licensed copy of a program on twenty computers is an example of
questions.explanation:
A licence allows a set number of installations. Using it on more computers than it allows breaks copyright: that is software piracy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- plagiarism: Plagiarism is passing off someone else's work or ideas as your own.
- hacking: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system.
- phishing: Phishing is tricking people into giving away passwords.

questions.stem: Which form of intellectual property protects a company's name, logo or slogan?
questions.explanation:
A trademark is a registered name, symbol, logo or slogan that identifies a company's goods or services.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a patent: A patent protects a new invention.
- copyright: Copyright protects original creative works such as books, music and software.
- a licence: A licence is permission to use something, not a form of protection.

questions.stem: Copying paragraphs from a website into an assignment without quotation marks or a reference is
questions.explanation:
Plagiarism is presenting another person's words or ideas as your own. Use your own words, put quotes in quotation marks and cite the source.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- software piracy: Piracy is the illegal copying of software.
- netiquette: Netiquette is good manners online.
- data protection: Data protection is the safe and fair handling of personal data.

questions.stem: Typing a whole message in CAPITAL LETTERS is considered poor netiquette because it
questions.explanation:
Online, capital letters are read as shouting, which is rude; netiquette asks users to write politely and normally.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- spreads computer viruses: Capital letters cannot carry a virus.
- breaks copyright law: Capital letters have nothing to do with copyright.
- cannot be read by email programs: Email programs show capital letters normally.

options.label: D
options.content: cannot be read by email programs

questions.stem: Repeatedly sending threatening or insulting messages to a classmate on social media is
questions.explanation:
Cyberbullying uses phones and online tools to threaten, embarrass or exclude someone. Victims should save evidence, block, report and tell a trusted adult.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- spam: Spam is unwanted bulk messages, usually advertising.
- identity theft: Identity theft is pretending to be someone else to commit fraud.
- encryption: Encryption is scrambling data to keep it secret.

questions.stem: The trail of posts, photos and other information a person leaves on the Internet is called their
questions.explanation:
A digital footprint can last for years and can be seen by future schools and employers, so think before posting.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- digital divide: The digital divide is the gap between people with and without access to ICT.
- password: A password is a secret word used to log in.
- IP address: An IP address is the number that identifies a device on a network.

questions.stem: A set of rules that students agree to follow when using a school's computers and Internet connection is
questions.explanation:
An acceptable use policy (AUP) sets out how an organisation's computers, network and Internet may be used, such as using only your own account and not installing software.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a licence agreement: A licence agreement sets the terms for using one piece of software.
- a patent: A patent protects an invention.
- a firewall: A firewall is security hardware or software, not a set of rules for users.

papers.title: Computer Viruses and Cybersecurity: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on computer viruses and cybersecurity, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Malware that spreads across networks by itself, without attaching to a file, is a
questions.explanation:
Worms copy themselves from computer to computer across networks without any user action, often slowing networks down.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- virus: A virus needs to attach to a file that is opened or run.
- Trojan horse: A Trojan relies on the user installing it, and does not copy itself.
- cookie: A cookie is a small text file a website stores; it is not malware.

questions.stem: A free game that secretly gives an attacker control of the computer once installed is an example of
questions.explanation:
Like the wooden horse of the Greek story, a Trojan looks harmless or useful but carries something hostile inside.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a worm: A worm spreads by itself; it does not need to look like a useful program.
- adware: Adware shows unwanted advertisements.
- a firewall: A firewall protects a computer; it is not malware.

questions.stem: Malware that encrypts a user's files and demands payment to unlock them is
questions.explanation:
Ransomware such as WannaCry (2017) locks or encrypts files and demands a ransom. Regular backups mean the files can be restored without paying.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- spyware: Spyware secretly records activity; it does not lock files.
- adware: Adware shows advertisements.
- a keylogger: A keylogger records keystrokes to steal passwords.

questions.stem: An SMS claiming to be from a bank, asking the receiver to reply with their PIN to avoid their account being closed, is an example of
questions.explanation:
Phishing uses fake messages that pretend to come from trusted organisations, often with urgent threats, to trick people into revealing passwords or PINs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- hacking a firewall: No firewall is involved; the message tricks the person.
- a denial-of-service attack: A DoS attack floods a server with requests.
- encryption: Encryption protects data; it is not an attack.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest password?
questions.explanation:
A strong password is long and mixes upper- and lower-case letters, digits and symbols, and is not a name, date or common word.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- password123: A common word with simple digits is guessed in seconds.
- Aminata2008: A name with a birth year is easy to guess.
- 12345678: A simple number sequence is among the first passwords attackers try.

questions.stem: Scrambling data so that only someone with the correct key can read it is called
questions.explanation:
Encryption turns readable data into code; with the key it can be turned back. It protects passwords, messages and web pages sent over HTTPS.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- compression: Compression makes files smaller; it does not hide them.
- backup: A backup is a spare copy of data.
- formatting: Formatting prepares or erases a storage device.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the FIRST thing to do when a computer is found to be infected with malware?
questions.explanation:
Disconnecting stops the malware spreading and sending data. Then scan with up-to-date antivirus software, change passwords from a clean device, and restore files from backups.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- reinstall the operating system: Reinstalling is a last resort if scanning and cleaning fail.
- share the files with friends to save them: Sharing infected files spreads the malware.
- switch off the antivirus program: The antivirus is needed to find and remove the malware.

options.label: B
options.content: share the files with friends to save them

options.label: C
options.content: disconnect it from the Internet and the network
